Learning Objectives
Understand imaging modalities available for the evaluation of the hip.
Understand the diagnosis and parameters of structural hip deformities, such as
developmental dysplasia of the hip and cam and pincer deformities, via imaging studies.
Understand the diagnosis and parameters of common etiologies of hip pain, such as
degenerative arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, osteonecrosis, and idiopathic transient
osteoporosis of the hip, via imaging studies.
Overview
Hip pain may result from various etiologies, including structural abnormality, traumatic injury,
degenerative joint disease, inflammatory arthritis, and osteonecrosis.

Accurate diagnosis of hip pathology is a challenge and requires a thorough patient history and
physical examination.
Radiographic evaluation is vital to the diagnostic workup of patients with hip pain.

Overview
Various conditions can result in hip pain, and a thorough patient history and physical
examination are necessary to make an accurate diagnosis. Patient demographics, the
mechanism of injury, symptom chronicity, and risk factors should be elucidated during
the clinic visit. Radiographic evaluation of the hip is a necessary adjunct to accurately
diagnose and manage hip pathology. Multiple imaging modalities exist for thorough
radiographic evaluation, and findings should correlate with patient symptoms. In
addition to assisting with diagnosis and management, radiographic evaluation may
facilitate postoperative monitoring after surgical management, such as total hip
arthroplasty (THA).
Imaging Studies
Plain Radiography
Plain radiography is the initial imaging modality. Plain radiographs allow for evaluation of
osseous structures of the hip via multiple views.
AP pelvis view
This view is performed with the x-ray beam centered between the superior border of the
pubic symphysis and a line connecting the anterior superior iliac spines. Internal rotation of
the lower extremities by 15° maximizes the length of the femoral neck, given native femoral
anteversion.
Ideal imaging should show symmetric iliac wings and obturator foramen. The distance
between the superior border of the pubic symphysis and the tip of the coccyx should be
approximately 1 to 3 cm (Figure 1; Resource 1).
A weight-bearing view can be obtained to better visualize loss of joint space.
Systematic evaluation of an AP pelvis view involves accurate assessment of osseous
landmarks, including the ilioischial line; the iliopectineal line; and the anterior and posterior

Figure 1 AP pelvic radiograph demonstrates symmetric iliac wings and obturator foramen,

Plain Radiography
Plain radiography often is the first imaging modality performed in the work up of
patients with hip pathology. The AP pelvis view is a coronal image of the pelvis and
captures both hip joints. A weight-bearing radiograph is ideal for the accurate
measurement of joint space1 (Resource 2). Proper rotation of the pelvis is visualized by
the symmetric appearance of the iliac wings and obturator foramen. In addition, the
coccyx should be approximately 1 to 3 cm superior to the superior border of the pubic
symphysis for appropriate tilt2 (Resource 3).

Systematic evaluation of AP pelvic radiographs is crucial, and many imaging landmarks
have been described. The ilioischial and iliopectineal lines represent the posterior and
anterior columns of the acetabulum, respectively. The anterior and posterior walls of the
acetabulum should be evaluated for fracture or abnormal morphology. The sourcil, or
weight-bearing surface of the acetabulum, should be assessed. The teardrop represents
the medial acetabulum at the level of the acetabular fossa. Abnormalities in any of these
structures may indicate a pathologic process. The proximal femur, including the femoral
head, femoral neck, and trochanteric region, also can be evaluated.
Judet views: oblique radiographs of the pelvis obtained to better assess pathology
involving the acetabulum. It is obtained with the pelvis in 45° of rotation (Figure 2)
Iliac oblique view
Visualizes the posterior column and the anterior wall of the acetabulum
Obturator oblique view
Visualizes the anterior column and the posterior wall of the acetabulum

Figure 2 Judet radiograph of a pelvis demonstrates an obturator oblique view of the
right hemipelvis and an iliac oblique view of the left hemipelvis. (Image courtesy of Vasili
Karas, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Judet views of the pelvis are oblique radiographs used to better evaluate the acetabulum
and are obtained with 45° of rotation in both directions. A single image will obtain an
obturator oblique view of one hemipelvis and an iliac oblique view of the contralateral
hemipelvis. The obturator oblique radiograph is obtained for the evaluation of the
anterior column and posterior wall of the acetabulum. The iliac oblique radiograph is
obtained for the evaluation of the posterior column and the anterior wall of the
acetabulum. These radiographs are useful in characterizing pathology of the
acetabulum, such as fracture, neoplasm, and infectious pathology. In addition, Judet
radiographs may assist in characterizing acetabular osteolysis or pelvic discontinuity
after THA.

Lateral views: defines the osseous anatomy of the proximal femur, the anterior and
posterior joint spaces, and the acetabular rims (Resource 1)
A cross-table lateral view is obtained with the patient supine. The unaffected limb is
flexed at the hip to 90°, the affected limb is rotated internally 15°, and the beam is
positioned parallel to the table at an angle of 45° and centered on the femoral head
(Figure 3).
Figure 3 Cross-table lateral radiograph of a hip obtained with the x-ray beam parallel to
the table, angled 45°, and centered on the femoral head. The patient is in the supine
position, the unaffected limb is flexed 90°, and the affected limb is in 15° of internal
rotation. (Reproduced from Shah RR, Bohnenkamp FC: Radiographic evaluation of the
hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 407-416.)
Dunn and modified Dunn views are performed at angles of 90° and 45° of hip flexion,
respectively. The patient is in the supine position, the affected limb is abducted 20°
with neutral rotation, and the beam is placed between the anterior superior iliac spine
and the pubic symphysis perpendicular to the table (Figure 4).

Multiple lateral radiographic views of the hip have been described to assess morphology
of the femoral head and neck. The cross-table lateral view is useful in the trauma setting
to decrease the risk of fracture displacement. In addition, patients with hip pathology
may not be able to tolerate the positions required for other lateral views secondary to
pain or restricted range of motion. The cross-table lateral view also can be used to
assess acetabular component positioning after THA.
A Dunn lateral radiograph is obtained with the affected hip in 90° of hip flexion, 20° of
abduction, and neutral rotation. If the patient is unable to achieve 90o of hip flexion, a

modified Dunn view can be obtained with the hip in 45° of flexion. The frog-lateral view
is obtained with the knee flexed to 30° to 40° and the hip abducted 45°. The false-profile
view is obtained with the patient standing. The affected hip is placed against the
cassette, and the ipsilateral foot is placed parallel to the cassette with the pelvis rotated
65°. A false-profile view facilitates assessment of acetabular morphology2 (Resource 3).
Computed Tomography
Cross-sectional imaging study that uses ionizing radiation to produce images with enhanced
bony detail in multiple planes
CT can accurately determine acetabular and femoral morphology independent of patient
positioning.
Three-dimensional reconstructions can be performed easily, which may assist in preoperative
surgical planning.
Postoperative CT can be performed to evaluate for postoperative complications such as
nonunion or malunion in the fracture setting, to characterize osteolysis, and to determine
component positioning after THA.

Computed Tomography
CT provides cross-sectional images with enhanced osseous detail in multiple planes. CT
enables improved assessment of osseous pathology, such as fracture displacement,
fracture extension, osseous cysts, neoplasms, infections, or ossification of soft-tissue
structures3 (Resource 3). Multiplanar imaging and enhanced osseous details allow for
accurate assessment of acetabular and femoral morphology. In addition, three-
dimensional reconstructions can be performed to create anatomic models that aid in
diagnosis and preoperative planning. Postoperative CT may aid in the diagnosis of
nonunion and malunion after fracture fixation. CT also can be used to characterize
periprosthetic osteolysis, fracture, and component positioning after THA.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging

MRI produces cross-sectional images without ionizing radiation.
MRI provides high-contrast resolution that enables enhanced imaging of soft-tissue structures
and the detection of bone marrow changes.
Magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) involves the intra-articular injection of gadolinium
contrast under fluoroscopic or ultrasonographic guidance to enhance the assessment of intra-
articular structures.
Metal artifact reduction sequence MRI is useful for imaging in patients with metallic implants
to limit the amount of artifact produced (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Axial, T1-weighted metal artifact reduction sequence MRI of a right hip shows a large
hyperintense, heterogeneous fluid collection or pseudotumor (arrow) extending from the hip
joint into the anteromedial thigh. (Reproduced from Bolognesi MP, Ledford CK: Metal-on-metal
total hip arthroplasty: Patient evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2015;23[12]:724-
731.)


Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is an advanced imaging modality that produces cross-sectional images in multiple
planes using a strong magnetic field that avoids ionizing radiation. MRI produces images
with high-contrast resolution that allow for evaluation of intra-articular and extra-
articular soft-tissue structures, including tendons, ligaments, and cartilage. In addition,
MRI is associated with a high degree of sensitivity for detecting early pathologic
processes affecting bone marrow, such as stress fractures, occult fractures, infection,
osteonecrosis, and neoplasms. MRA involves an intra-articular injection of dilute contrast
material to further evaluate for intra-articular pathology, such as cartilage defects and
labral tears4 (Resource 4). Metal artifact reduction sequence MRI is a method used to
reduce the size and intensity of imaging artifact produced by metallic implants, such as
THA components, and is useful in evaluating for periprosthetic pathologies, such as
pseudotumor formation, or the integrity of the abductors5 (Resource 5).
Specific Imaging Findings
Radiographic Parameters of Osteoarthritis
Plain radiographs often are sufficient for the evaluation of osteoarthritis.
Characterized by joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and
subchondral cysts
Degenerative arthritic changes observed on an AP pelvis view can be classified according to
Tönnis grades.
Grade 0 demonstrates a normal joint space with no arthritic changes (Figure 8).
Grade 1 demonstrates slight joint space narrowing, increasing subchondral sclerosis of the
acetabulum and/or femoral head, and mild osteophyte formation (Figure 9).
Grade 2 demonstrates small cysts in the head or acetabulum, moderate joint-space
narrowing, and loss of sphericity of the femoral head (Figure 10).
Grade 3 demonstrates large cysts in the femoral head or acetabulum, severe joint-space
narrowing or obliteration, and severe deformity of the femoral head (Figure 11).
Preoperative templating for THA can be performed on AP pelvic radiographs to assess for
limb-length discrepancy and to estimate component size and position.

Radiographic Parameters of Osteoarthritis
Primary osteoarthritis is the progressive loss of articular cartilage, leading to joint
degeneration. It is commonly observed in the elderly population. However, degeneration
of the hip can occur at an earlier age secondary to other conditions, such as structural
deformity leading to arthritic changes. Patients with a history of traumatic injury to the
hip joint also are at risk for posttraumatic arthritis at a young age.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:57 PM
AAOS | Radiographic Evaluation of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002009
16/44

Osteoarthritis of the hip is well-visualized on plain radiographs. Findings include joint
space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and subchondral cysts.
The Tönnis classification is a simple qualitative system used to grade the degree of
degenerative changes. Grade 0 demonstrates a normal joint space with no arthritic
changes. Grade 1 demonstrates slight joint space narrowing, marginal osteophyte
formation, and subchondral sclerosis of the femoral head and/or acetabulum. Grade 2
demonstrates moderate joint space narrowing, small bone cyst formation, and loss of
femoral head sphericity. Grade 3 demonstrates large cyst formation, severe joint space
narrowing, and severe deformity of the femoral head6 (Resource 6).
An AP pelvic radiograph obtained with a calibrated reference marker also can be used
for preoperative templating for THA. Limb-length discrepancy can be measured by
creating a horizontal reference line between the base of the bilateral teardrops or the
inferior aspects of the bilateral ischial tuberosities. The difference in distance from this
reference line to each lesser trochanter represents the estimated limb-length
discrepancy. Acetabular overlays are used to estimate acetabular reaming, component
position and size, and the center of rotation of the prosthetic joint. Femoral overlays are
used to estimate the osteotomy site, component size, neck length, and offset7 (Resource
7).
Radiographic Parameters of Inflammatory Arthritis
The most common cause of inflammatory arthritis is rheumatoid arthritis. Other causes
include seronegative arthritis, such as psoriatic arthritis; ankylosing spondylitis; and
enteropathic arthropathies.
Similar to degenerative arthritis, plain radiographs often are sufficient for the evaluation of
inflammatory arthritis.
Signs of inflammatory arthritis include periarticular erosion, osteopenia, and concentric
erosion of the hip, with minimal osteophyte formation.
Protrusio acetabuli and coxa profunda also are characteristic of inflammatory arthritis.

Radiographic Parameters of Inflammatory Arthritis

Inflammatory arthritis encompasses a group of systemic inflammatory conditions that
cause synovial inflammation, resulting in articular destruction. The most common cause
of inflammatory arthritis is rheumatoid arthritis; however, other etiologies exist, such as
ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and enteropathic arthropathies. Inflammatory
arthritis of the hip also results in the destruction of articular cartilage and joint space
narrowing; however, signs of inflammatory arthritis observed on radiograph may aid in
distinguishing the inflammatory origin of these conditions from that of degenerative
osteoarthritis. Inflammatory arthritis typically results in the uniform and concentric loss
of articular cartilage, relative osteopenia, minimal osteophyte formation, and the
presence of periarticular erosion8 (Resource 8). In addition, inflammatory arthritis is
associated with coxa profunda or protrusio acetabuli. Coxa profunda indicates that the
medial wall of the acetabulum is at or medial to the ilioischial line. Protrusio acetabuli
indicates that the femoral head also is medial to the ilioischial line. Protrusio acetabuli
also may be associated with osteomalacia, fibrous dysplasia, osteogenesis imperfecta,
pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement (FAI), and Paget disease.
Radiographic Parameters of Osteonecrosis
Plain Radiographs
Osteonecrosis is best visualized on frog-lateral plain radiographs. It manifests as a radiolucent
lesion with a sclerotic rim in the superolateral aspect of the femoral head (Figure 12).
Osteonecrosis may result in subchondral collapse, as identified by the crescent sign (Figure
13). In patients with progressive disease, the femoral head may collapse and result in articular
cartilage degeneration, showing the signs of secondary osteoarthritis.
The Ficat classification (based on standard radiographs) is used to stage osteonecrosis of the
femoral head.
Stage 0: preclinical and preradiographic stage
Stage I: symptomatic, normal radiographs
Stage II: sclerosis, cysts, diffuse porosis
Stage III: femoral head collapse, the crescent sign, broken contour of the femoral head
Stage IV: osteoarthritis, femoral head flattening

Plain Radiographs
Osteonecrosis of the hip is defined as the death of the femoral head because of a lack of
blood supply. It can progress to femoral head collapse and joint degeneration. Plain
radiographs of patients with very early stages of the disease may appear normal. As the
disease progresses, the initial findings of osteonecrosis, including sclerosis and cystic
changes of the femoral head, are best visualized on frog-lateral radiographs. In patients
with late-stage disease, femoral head collapse and degenerative changes are observed.

The Ficat classification has been used to describe the plain radiographic findings of
osteonecrosis of the femoral head. Stage 0 disease is preclinical, with normal
radiographs. Stage I disease indicates the development of symptoms; however, no
findings are observed on plain radiographs. Stage II disease demonstrates early
radiographic findings, including sclerosis, cyst formation, and/or relative osteoporosis of
the femoral head. Stage III disease is characterized by the development of the crescent
sign, representing the collapse of subchondral bone. Stage IV disease demonstrates the
progressive loss of articular cartilage and femoral head flattening9 (Resource 9).
MRI
MRI is associated with a high sensitivity and a high specificity for the diagnosis of osteonecrosis
and is especially useful if radiographs are negative. The bilateral hips should be included
because of the risk of bilateral disease.
The University of Pennsylvania Classification described by Steinberg is a plain radiographic
classification system that also includes MRI findings.
The following parameters can predict potential collapse of the femoral head.
The modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle represents the combined value of the angle
of necrosis in the midsagittal and midcoronal planes (Figure 14).
Less than 190° = low risk
190° to 240° = moderate risk (50%)
Greater than 240° = high risk (near 100%)
The percentage of femoral head involvement observed on MRI can be used to estimate the
risk of collapse.
Less than 30% = low risk (5% collapse at 5 years)
30% to 50% = moderate risk (46% collapse at 5 years)
Greater than 50% = high risk (83% collapse at 5 years)

MRI
MRI is useful in the early stages of disease, if plain radiographic findings are not evident,
because MRI is highly sensitive and highly specific in the diagnosis of osteonecrosis.
Findings include a low signal intensity band on T1-weighted images. T2-weighted images
demonstrate a double line sign, which has two concentric low and high signal bands. MRI
has largely replaced bone scanning in the diagnosis of osteonecrosis.
The University of Pennsylvania classification described by Steinberg is similar to the Ficat
classification but uses MRI to further delineate the stage and grade of disease. Stage 0 is
defined by normal radiographs and MRI. Stage I is defined by normal radiographs, but
abnormal MRI findings are observed. Stage I disease can be further stratified to grade A,
mild disease with less than 15% of the head affected; grade B, moderate disease with
15% to 30% of the head affected; and grade C, severe disease with more than 30% of the
head affected. Stage II is defined by cystic and sclerotic changes in the femoral head and

abnormal MRI findings. Stage II disease is further stratified into grade A, mild disease
with less than 15% of the head affected; grade B, moderate disease with 15% to 30% of
the head affected; and grade C, severe disease with more than 30% of the head affected.
Stage III is defined by subchondral collapse (the crescent sign) without flattening of the
femoral head on plain radiographs and abnormal MRI findings. Stage III is further
stratified into grade A, mild disease with less than 15% of the head affected; grade B,
moderate disease with 15% to 30% of the head affected; and grade C, severe disease
with more than 30% of the head affected. The classic finding of stage IV disease is
flattening of the femoral head on plain radiographs and abnormal MRI findings. Stage IV
disease is further stratified into grade A, mild disease with less than 15% of the surface
affected and less than 2 mm of depression; grade B, moderate disease with 15% to 30%
of the surface affected and 2 mm to 4 mm of depression; and grade C, severe disease
with more than 30% of the surface affected and more than 4 mm of depression. Stage V
is defined by joint space narrowing on plain radiographs with abnormal MRI findings.
Stage VI osteonecrosis is defined by advanced degenerative changes10 (Resource 10).
In addition to providing diagnostic information in patients with negative radiographs,
MRI is useful in assessing the risk of potential collapse. Two methods have been
described. The modified Kerboul method uses the angle of necrosis on the midsagittal
and midcoronal images of the femoral head to produce a combined angle. Values less
than 190° indicate a low risk of collapse, values of 190° to 240° indicate a moderate risk
(approximately 50%) of collapse, and values of more than 240° indicate a high risk
(nearly 100%) of collapse. The second method uses the percentage of femoral head
involvement to predict the risk of femoral head collapse at 5-year follow-up. Less than
30% involvement of the femoral head represents a low risk of collapse (5%), involvement
of 30% to 50% of the femoral head represents a moderate risk of collapse (46%), and
more than 50% involvement of the femoral head represents a high risk of collapse
(83%)11 (Resource 11).
Idiopathic Transient Osteoporosis of the Hip
Idiopathic transient osteoporosis of the hip is a rare diagnosis that is associated with pain on
ambulation.

9/3/26, 5:57 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002009
23/44

Radiographic findings often are normal in patients in the early stages of disease. However,
radiographs may demonstrate diffuse osteopenia about the head and neck with preserved
joint space. These findings often are subtle and nonspecific.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosis (Figure 15).
MRI demonstrates diffuse marrow edema of the head and neck.
T1-weighted images demonstrate diffuse low signal intensity and loss of marrow.
T2-weighted images demonstrate high signal intensity in the marrow and a joint effusion.

Idiopathic Transient Osteoporosis of the Hip
Idiopathic transient osteoporosis of the hip is an uncommon self-limiting condition that
causes painful osteoporosis of the proximal femur. Plain radiographs often are normal,
especially in patients in the early stages of disease. Osteopenia of the femoral head and
neck with preserved joint space may be observed, however. Radiographic findings may
persist for as many as 2 years despite symptom resolution. Because of the subtle and
nonspecific findings observed on plain radiographs, MRI is the preferred imaging
modality for diagnosis. MRI demonstrates bone marrow edema of the femoral head and
neck that is visualized as low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal
intensity on T2-weighted or short tau inversion recovery images. A joint effusion may be
present and is best observed on T2-weighted images12 (Resource 12).

Plain Radiographs
DDH is defined as the abnormal development of the hip resulting in decreased
anterolateral femoral head coverage and leading to joint instability and subsequent
degeneration. DDH is associated with characteristic findings on plain radiographs, and
multiple measurements have been described to quantify femoral head coverage and
acetabular inclination. Superolateral coverage of the femoral head can be measured via
the LCEA, or angle of Wiberg. The LCEA is measured on an AP pelvis view by drawing a
vertical line from the center of the femoral head that is perpendicular to the transverse
pelvic axis. A second line is drawn from the center of the femoral head to the lateral
edge of the sourcil. The angle between these two lines is measured. An LCEA of 25° to

20° indicates dysplasia.
The anterior center-edge angle is measured via a false-profile view to assess anterior
acetabular coverage. The anterior center-edge angle is calculated by measuring the
angle between a vertical line drawn from the center of the femoral head to the anterior
acetabular edge and a second line drawn from the center of the femoral head to the
anterior acetabular edge. Angles of 25° to 40° are considered normal, whereas angles
less than 20° indicate dysplasia.
An increase in acetabular inclination (Tönnis angle) on an AP pelvic radiograph also is
observed in patients with DDH. Acetabular inclination is calculated by measuring the
angle between a horizontal line parallel to the transverse axis of the pelvis, starting at
the inferior aspect of the acetabular sourcil, and a line connecting the inferior aspect of
the sourcil to the lateral margin of the sourcil. Normal acetabular inclination is less than
10°, whereas angles greater than 10° indicate dysplasia.13
DDH is associated with abnormalities in acetabular version, which can be evaluated on
an AP pelvic radiograph. Normal anteversion of the acetabulum is visualized if the
anterior wall of the acetabulum converges with the line projected from the posterior rim
at the lateral sourcil. The crossover sign is identified if the lines representing the anterior
wall and the posterior wall cross before converging at the lateral sourcil, which indicates
relative acetabular retroversion or a deficient posterior wall. Increased visualization of
the ischial spine on a properly obtained AP pelvic radiograph is associated with
acetabular retroversion and is known as the prominent ischial spine sign (Resources 1
and 13)
Additional radiographic findings include abnormalities in the anatomy of the proximal
femur and hip center.
Proximal femur: a high neck-shaft angle (coxa valga) and increased proximal femoral
anteversion

relation to the ilioischial line; greater than 10 mm is considered lateralized.SEND FEEDBACK

In addition to structural deformity to the acetabulum, DDH is associated with structural
abnormalities of the proximal femur, including an increased neck-shaft angle, or coxa
valga. The normal neck-shaft angle of the proximal femur is 125°. Coxa valga often is
defined as a neck-shaft angle of more than 140°. In general, on an appropriately rotated
AP pelvic radiograph, the center of the femoral head should be at the same level as the
tip of the greater trochanter. An increase in the neck-shaft angle will appear as if the
center of the femoral head is superior to the greater trochanter; this appearance often is
used as a visual screen for coxa valga. In addition, DDH is associated with increased
proximal femoral anteversion, and the greater trochanter is observed more posterior.
This is difficult to assess on plain radiographs. CT scans can be obtained to further
evaluate for rotational deformity of the proximal femur and acetabulum. DDH is
associated with lateralization of the hip center, which can be observed on AP pelvic
radiographs. Lateralization of the hip center is defined as more than 10 mm between the
medial aspect of the femoral head and the ilioischial line.14,15

Classification
Crowe classification of DDH—Two measurements can be made: (1) the proximal migration of
the inferomedial femoral head-neck junction in relation to the height of the undeformed
femoral head or (2) the vertical displacement of the femoral head-neck junction in relation to
the overall height of the pelvis.
Type I: less than 50% proximal migration in relation to femoral head height or less than 10%
vertical displacement in relation to pelvic height
Type II: 50% to 75% proximal migration in relation to femoral head height or 10% to 15%
vertical displacement in relation to pelvic height
Type III: 75% to 100% proximal migration in relation to femoral head height or 16% to 20%
vertical displacement in relation to pelvic height
Type IV: greater than 100% proximal migration in relation to femoral head height or greater
than 20% vertical displacement in relation to pelvic height
Hartofilakidis classification
Dysplasia (type A): femoral head is contained within the true acetabulum; subluxation is
possible.
Low dislocation (type B): femoral head is dislocated and contained within a false acetabulum
that is continuous with the true acetabulum.
High dislocation (type C): femoral head is dislocated and contained within a false acetabulum
that is not continuous with the true acetabulum.

DDH is classified most often via the Crowe classification or the Hartofilakidis
classification. The Crowe classification can be quantified in one of two ways; both start
by drawing a reference line connecting the bilateral teardrops. The first method used in
the Crowe classification is the measurement of proximal migration of the inferomedial
femoral head-neck junction from the inter-teardrop line relative to the height of the
undeformed femoral head. The second method is the measurement of vertical

relation to the height of the pelvis. Type II is 50% to 75% of proximal migration in relation
to femoral head height or 10% to 15% of vertical displacement in relation to the height of
the pelvis. Type III is 75% to 100% of proximal migration in relation to femoral head
height or 16% to 20% of vertical displacement in relation to the height of the pelvis. Type
IV is more than 100% of proximal migration in relation to femoral head height or more
than 20% of vertical displacement in relation to the height of the pelvis.
The Hartofilakidis classification system is divided into three groups: dysplasia, low
dislocation, and high dislocation. Hips classified as dysplastic (type A) contain the
characteristics of hip dysplasia, and subluxation of the femoral head may be present;
however, the femoral head is contained within the true acetabulum. A low dislocation
(type B) occurs if the hip is dislocated and the femoral head articulates with a false
acetabulum; however, the false acetabulum is continuous and overlaps with the true
acetabulum. A high dislocation (type C) is observed if the hip is dislocated and the
femoral head articulates with a false acetabulum that is not continuous with the true
acetabulum14.
Radiographic Findings of FAI
FAI is abnormal contact between the femoral neck and the acetabulum, leading to damage of
the labrum and articular cartilage. It is a common etiology of secondary osteoarthritis
(Resource 14).

Cam Deformity
FAI is the result of aberrant morphology of the proximal femur and/or acetabulum,
resulting in dynamic impingement of the acetabular rim and the femoral neck. FAI leads
to damage of the acetabular labrum and the articular cartilage. It is a common cause of
secondary osteoarthritis of the hip. Three types of FAI exist, cam impingement, pincer
impingement, and combined impingement.
Cam impingement is the result of a femoral head-neck deformity, resulting in a
nonspherical femoral head, and is commonly observed in young, active males. AP and
lateral radiographs are used to evaluate a cam deformity. Lateral femoral head-neck
deformities can be observed on AP radiographs; however, deformities of the anterior,

anterolateral, or anterosuperior femoral head-neck junction are best evaluated on
lateral radiographs. A cam deformity has been described qualitatively as a pistol grip
deformity of the proximal femur, in which the femoral head has lost its sphericity, and
the femoral head-neck junction is no longer concave but flat or even convex.
Two important quantitative radiographic parameters of a cam deformity should be
assessed. First, the α angle is assessed to help quantify femoral head asphericity. Most
commonly, the position of the cam deformity is centered at the anterosuperior head-
neck junction. The α angle should be measured on a lateral radiograph, such as a Dunn
or modified Dunn view. Measurement begins by determining the best-fit perfect circle
centered over the femoral head. Next, a line is drawn from the center of the femoral
head and extends along the axis of the femoral neck. Another line is then drawn from
the center of the femoral head to the point at which the femoral head neck-junction
extends beyond the border of the previously drawn perfect circle, where the femoral
head loses its sphericity. Normal cutoff values for the α angle are controversial and
range from 42° to 63°. In general, an α angle greater than 50° may indicate the presence
of a cam deformity.
The HNO ratio should be calculated. Again, this ratio is best obtained using a lateral
radiograph. First, a line is drawn along the axis of the femoral neck for reference. Then, a
line is drawn parallel to the femoral neck axis at the anterolateral aspect of the femoral
head, and another parallel line is drawn at the anterolateral aspect of the femoral neck.
The distance between the last two lines drawn is known as HNO. The HNO ratio is
calculated by dividing the HNO by the diameter of the femoral head to standardize
according to femoral head size and radiographic magnification. An HNO ratio of less
than 0.17 is abnormal and indicative of a cam deformity.16

Pincer Deformity
Pincer impingement is a result of acetabular overcoverage and/or acetabular
retroversion, causing impingement of the acetabular rim on the femoral neck and
resulting in damage to the labrum. In addition, if the femoral neck impinges on the
anterior rim, the head is forcibly subluxated posteriorly and may lever out, resulting in a
contrecoup lesion on the articular cartilage.
Acetabular overcoverage may result from increased acetabular depth, which is visualized
on AP pelvic radiographs. Protrusio acetabuli may result in global overcoverage and a
pincer deformity. In addition, coxa profunda has been associated with a pincer
deformity; however, coxa profunda may be a normal anatomic variant and is not a
specific feature of FAI. Os acetabuli results from an unfused secondary ossification
center of the acetabulum and may result in focal overcoverage of the femoral head.
Radiographic measurement of the LCEA on an AP pelvic radiograph should be
performed to quantify lateral acetabular coverage. An LCEA greater than 40° represents
an abnormal value. In addition, acetabular inclination should be measured. Values less
than 0° represent a down-sloping sourcil, which is concerning for pincer deformity.
Acetabular retroversion is another source of deformity that may result in pincer-type FAI.
The crossover sign and prominent ischial spine sign are qualitative descriptions of
acetabular retroversion visualized on AP pelvic radiographs. The posterior wall sign
refers to a radiographic sign in which the center of the femoral head is located lateral to
the posterior wall on an AP pelvic radiograph. It is another qualitative assessment of

Advanced Imaging Studies: MRI/MRA
Aids in determining the specific location of the cam deformity, the extent of injury of the
chondral surface, and the labral damage from FAI
Labrum: a normal labrum is triangular shaped and displays a hypointense signal on MRA.
MRA is associated with a high sensitivity for the detection of labral pathology and often is the
preferred advanced imaging modality.
An abnormal hyperintense signal within the labrum may indicate a labral tear (Figure 23).
In cam impingement, an undersurface tear usually is present at the chondrolabral junction.
In pincer impingement, a longitudinal labral tear may be observed as a linear hyperintensity
in the labrum.
Cartilage: articular cartilage is examined for flap or shear injuries or indentations on the
femoral head or acetabular cartilage.
Contrast traversing from underneath the cartilage and subchondral bone and
communicating with the joint is consistent with a chondral tear.
Delayed gadolinium-enhanced MRI of cartilage (dGEMRIC) better delineates articular cartilage
damage by measuring the remaining glycosaminoglycan content.
dGEMRIC has prognostic value in predicting patient responses to hip preservation osteotomy
procedures.

MRI commonly is used to evaluate patients with FAI. Measurement of the α angle was
originally described using MRI and may provide additional information regarding the size
and location of cam impingement deformities. MRI can be performed further
characterize acetabular anatomy with accurate assessment of acetabular version and
depth. These factors are important in preoperative planning for hip preservation
surgery.

A major advantage of MRI is the ability to use intra-articular gadolinium contrast in MRA,
which is associated with better sensitivity in the detection of labral pathology associated
with FAI. The labrum appears as a hypointense, triangular-shaped structure at the rim of
the acetabulum. A tear within the labrum is visualized as a hyperintense signal within the
labrum as intra-articular contrast extravasates within the tear. Cam impingement is
associated with an undersurface tear of the labrum, usually at the chondrolabral
junction. Pincer impingement is associated with a longitudinal labral tear, observed as a
linear hyperintensity in the labrum.
The integrity of the articular cartilage also can be evaluated. The generalized appearance
of the articular cartilage should be assessed. Severe degenerative changes can be
observed, with widespread loss of cartilage, which preclude hip preservation surgery. In
addition, articular shear injuries resulting in cartilage delamination may be identified by
the presence of contrast traversing underneath the cartilage and subchondral bone on
MRA. Biochemical MRI has been reported to detect early cartilage damage in patients
with FAI. For example, dGEMRIC can be performed to obtain information about the
proteoglycan-glycosaminoglycan content of cartilage. Abnormalities on dGEMRIC
imaging studies may help predict patient outcomes after hip preservation procedures
(Resources 14 and 15).
